extracted.intended_audience: employers, industry stakeholders, labor organizations, legal counsel, state plan administrators, and public commenters participating in OSHA rulemaking on heat injury and illness prevention
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts the legal, evidentiary, and programmatic criteria OSHA uses to justify and design a proposed federal Heat Injury and Illness Prevention standard, including statutory tests (significant risk, feasibility), required plan elements, coverage, and ancillary regulatory analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority: "reasonably necessary or appropriate" standard
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA is proposing the standard pursuant to the Occupational Safety and Health Act of 1970. The Act authorizes the agency to issue safety or health standards that are “reasonably necessary or appropriate” to provide safe or healthful employment and places of employment (29 U.S.C. 652(8)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A standard is reasonably necessary or appropriate when a significant risk of material harm exists in the workplace and the standard would substantially reduce or eliminate that workplace risk. Applicable legal requirements are discussed in Section II (Pertinent Legal Authority).

rubrics_metrics.name: Significant Risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Standards must address a significant risk of material harm that exists in the workplace (citing Benzene and related case law). OSHA's risk assessments are based on the best available evidence and final conclusions consider all information in the rulemaking record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts require substantial evidence and a reasoned explanation. OSHA may rely on “a body of reputable scientific thought” and use conservative assumptions, risking “error on the side of overprotection.” The determination is not a mathematical straitjacket and is largely policy-driven. See Benzene; Asbestos II; Nat'l Mining Ass'n.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technological Feasibility
rubrics_metrics.description: A standard is technologically feasible when the protective measures it requires already exist, when available technology can bring the protective measures into existence, or when that technology is reasonably likely to develop.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts interpret this to mean a typical firm in each affected industry or application group will reasonably be able to implement the requirements in most operations most of the time. OSHA may adopt “technology forcing” standards provided it gives industry reasonable time to develop new technologies. (Lead I; Lead II; Public Citizen v. OSHA)

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic Feasibility
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA must demonstrate that its standards are economically feasible — i.e., industry can absorb or pass on costs of compliance without threatening long-term profitability or the competitive structure of an industry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A reviewing court examines compliance cost estimates in relation to industry financial health and effects on consumer prices. OSHA must construct a reasonable estimate of compliance costs and likely effects; estimates need not be precise but must be adequately explained. Standards may impose significant costs so long as they do not cause massive economic dislocations or imperil industry existence. (Lead I; Lead II; Cotton Dust)

rubrics_metrics.name: High Degree of Employee Protection (Safety Standard Requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Safety standards must provide a high degree of employee protection to be consistent with the purpose of the Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because occupational heat effects addressed here are generally acute (heat stroke, heat exhaustion, heat syncope, injuries due to fatigue), the proposed standard is characterized as a safety standard. Addressing acute hazards is expected also to protect against potential chronic outcomes. (Lockout/Tagout I; Grain Dust)

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to create a Heat Injury and Illness Prevention Plan
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed rule is a programmatic standard that requires employers to create a heat injury and illness prevention plan to evaluate and control heat hazards in their workplace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan is a core program element to evaluate hazards and implement controls; OSHA sought input on alternatives and potential exclusions. The proposed standard provides flexibility for employers to choose control measures suited to their workplace, which can aid small organizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification of Heat Hazards
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers must identify heat hazards in the workplace as part of the prevention plan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hazard identification includes recognizing indoor and outdoor heat sources, heat-generating processes (e.g., hot tar ovens, furnaces), PPE that decreases cooling, and workplace practices or incentives that encourage working through heat exposure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engineering and Work Practice Controls at Two Heat Trigger Levels
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed standard establishes requirements for implementing engineering and work practice control measures at or above two heat trigger levels (an initial heat trigger and a high heat trigger).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA demonstrates the efficacy of these controls in reducing heat-related injury and illness (see Risk Reduction). The two-trigger approach prescribes escalating measures tied to measured/assessed heat conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heat Illness and Emergency Response Plan
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers must develop and implement a heat illness and emergency response plan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan must include procedures for recognizing and responding to heat-related emergencies and ensuring prompt medical attention. OSHA identified failures in past fatalities (e.g., employees left alone, inadequate medical attention) that such plans should address.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training for Employees and Supervisors
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed rule requires employers to provide training to employees and supervisors on heat hazards and prevention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Training should cover signs and symptoms of heat-related illness; prevention measures such as rest, hydration, shade; acclimatization; and employer procedures. OSHA cited NIOSH recommendations and campaign materials emphasizing training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recordkeeping and Retention
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed rule requires employers to retain records related to the heat prevention program.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recordkeeping supports enforcement, program evaluation, and tracking exposures and incidents; supporting materials are available in the rulemaking docket (Document ID OSHA-2021-0009).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and Application (Coverage of Employers and Sectors)
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed rule would apply to all employers conducting outdoor and indoor work in all general industry, construction, maritime, and agriculture sectors, with some exceptions (see Scope & Application).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA seeks input on alternatives and potential exclusions. State Plan requirements and interactions with State standards are addressed (requirements for States with OSHA-approved State Plans).

rubrics_metrics.name: Flexibility for Employers and Small Entities
rubrics_metrics.description: Many provisions provide flexibility for affected employers to choose control measures most suited to their workplace; this flexibility may be particularly beneficial to small organizations with limited resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA followed SBREFA procedures and convened a SBAR Panel; it considered Small Entity Representatives' (SERs) comments and conducted an Initial Regulatory Flexibility Analysis (see Section VIII.F.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory and Procedural Analyses and Requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA must perform ancillary analyses and comply with additional statutory and executive order requirements (e.g., Unfunded Mandates Reform Act, Tribal Consultation under EO 13175, consultation with ACCSH, Environmental Impacts, Consensus Standards, Incorporation by Reference, Protection of Children from Environmental Health Risks, Federalism, Paperwork Reduction Act review by OMB).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These additional requirements shape the NPRM content and analyses (see Section X. Additional Requirements; Section VIII Preliminary Economic Analysis and Initial Regulatory Flexibility Analysis). Supporting materials are in the public docket.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Best Available Evidence and Accounting for Underreporting
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA's risk assessments and significant risk determinations are based on the best available evidence and consider the rulemaking record; OSHA recognizes substantial undercounting in BLS and occupational data and accounts for this in its analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA cites evidence that BLS SOII undercounts and that workers' compensation data may show 3–6 times more cases. The agency discusses reasons for underreporting (e.g., disincentives to report, misattribution of symptoms) and considers these limitations in estimating risk and benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of Existing Standards, Guidance, and Consensus Documents
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA reviews and considers existing Federal, State, and non-governmental standards, guidance, and consensus documents (e.g., NIOSH criteria documents, ACGIH TLVs, State heat standards such as California, Washington, Oregon, Colorado, Minnesota).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The NPRM references prior NIOSH criteria (1972, 1986, 2016), State regulations, ACGIH TLVs, and other guidance to inform proposed provisions (e.g., rest breaks, hydration, shade, acclimatization, WBGT measurement).

rubrics_metrics.name: General Duty Clause Enforcement Elements
rubrics_metrics.description: When enforcing heat hazards without a specific standard, OSHA uses section 5(a)(1) (the General Duty Clause). To prove a violation, OSHA must establish: (1) the employer failed to keep the workplace free of a hazard to which employees were exposed; (2) the hazard was recognized; (3) the hazard was causing or likely to cause death or serious injury; and (4) a feasible means to eliminate or materially reduce the hazard existed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA has used the General Duty Clause for decades to cite heat hazards and documents historical citation data. The element list (including case citations) defines enforcement burdens absent a specific standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicators of Employer Program Failures from Fatality Investigations
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA identified recurring circumstances in heat-related fatality investigations (2017–2022) that indicate programmatic failures: employees left alone after symptoms started; employers not providing adequate medical attention; employers preventing rest breaks; employers not providing water on-site; employers not providing on-site access to shade; employers not providing cooling measures on-site; and employers not having acclimatization programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These specific failures inform the proposed standard's required elements (e.g., access to water/shade, rest breaks, acclimatization, medical response) and illustrate the kinds of employer obligations the rule seeks to remedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions and Key Terms (for consistent application)
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA defines key terms used throughout the proposal, including: heat stress (combined load from metabolic and environmental heat and heat retention), heat strain (the body's response to heat stress), heat-related illness (adverse clinical outcomes like heat exhaustion or heat stroke), and heat-related injury (an injury linked to heat exposure, such as a fall or cut).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistent definitions support hazard identification, measurement, and applicability of control measures; OSHA references ACGIH and NIOSH terminology (e.g., WBGT, RAL, REL).
